name: Priya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm operations lead at Westholm, a family company farm. Four hundred hectares of potatoes, sugar beet and wheat, plus a three-hundred-sow pig unit. I've got eight people under me. Day starts at half six with a stand-up in the yard office, then I'm between the pig unit and the fields all day, and I do the planning on my phone in between.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned planning on your phone. Is AI part of that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to plan the spray windows, draft the staff rota, read the soil sensor data. This year I talked the family into trialling a weeding robot on twelve hectares of beet. It missed a few rows, but it cut our hand-hoeing bill by about a third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and that's all it was ever going to be for most people. I'd probably post our weeding robot numbers on a farming forum, because they'd still be good. Less hype, more results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my edge, really. I already use this stuff more than anyone round here. In a flat world that still counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with the weeding robot, push to extend it to the full beet area next spring. Keep using the AI for planning. I'd probably look at a drone for crop scouting too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the farm where you'd still want more help from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the pigs. Tail biting, ventilation, early signs of illness. A camera that spots a coughing pig before I do would save more money than any robot in the potato field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this picture change anything for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small. Maybe a few hundred quid more a year if I take on more responsibility. It doesn't change my life.

S0.say: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and that's all it was going to be for most people. I'd post our weeding robot results on a farming forum, because they'd still be good.
S0.think: I think I keep my edge, since I already use these tools more than anyone nearby. In a flat world that still counts for something.
S0.do: Extends the weeding robot to the full beet area next spring and keeps using AI for planning. Looks at buying a drone for crop scouting.
S0.feel: Calm, with a touch of restlessness.
S0.quote: A camera that spots a coughing pig before I do would save more money than any robot in the potato field.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is already further along than most farmers and talks in results and percentages. Her most practical idea is cameras for early illness in the pig unit. A flat AI future would leave her slightly restless rather than relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the good farms pull ahead. If you're not learning it now, you'll be paying someone else to do it in five years. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, and some who wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do well. I know the kit, I know the software, and I'm on a farm big enough to afford it. The question is whether I stay an employee or start doing this for other farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Westholm to put robots in the pig unit for cleaning and monitoring, about sixty thousand, with my figures to back it. On the side I'd offer weekend drone scouting to smaller farms nearby, maybe fifty pounds a hectare. And I'd keep taking every course the dealers run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, my pig unit lead. He's 50 and hates his phone. I'd want him on board early, because he knows the sows better than any camera. If I automate Marcus out, I lose the one person who'd tell me when the robot is lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you set up the side business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very carefully, and not until I've got ten regular customers. I've got about four months saved, which is fine for a side thing. It's not enough to quit on.

S1.say: I'd say this is where the good farms pull ahead, and anyone not learning it now will be paying someone else to do it later. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I know the kit and work on a farm big enough to afford it. The real question is whether I stay an employee or work for other farms too.
S1.do: Pushes the farm to put around sixty thousand of cleaning and monitoring robots in the pig unit, backed by her figures. Starts weekend drone scouting for smaller farms at about fifty pounds a hectare and takes every dealer course.
S1.quote: If I automate Marcus out, I lose the one person who'd tell me when the robot is lying.
S1.fieldNote: Priya sees steady change as an opening and is already planning a side business. She values her older pig unit lead Marcus as a check on the machines, not a cost. She's careful about money: four months saved is enough for a side venture, not for leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot faster than anyone's ready for, including me. I'd still say get on board, because there's no other option. But I'd stop telling people it'll all be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my little drone business gets crushed. The big contractors with money would buy fleets of robots and do every farm in the county for less than I could. And Westholm wouldn't need an operations lead when the operations run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person running Westholm's whole robot fleet, starting this month. I'd keep the side business going but not borrow a penny for it. And I'd bump savings from four months towards six, because I can't see past 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm normally the calm one, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're usually ahead of the curve. What does two years do to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what bothers me. I've always been the early one, but in two years being early is just being slightly less late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably. She's a pharmacist, so she'd be in the same boat. We'd joke about it on the phone and then both go quiet.

S2.say: I'd say it's faster than anyone's ready for, including me, but there's still no option except getting on board. I'd stop telling people it will all be fine.
S2.think: I think big contractors with money would buy robot fleets and crush my small drone business. The farm wouldn't need an operations lead once the operations run themselves.
S2.do: Makes herself the person running the farm's whole robot fleet, starting immediately. Keeps the side business going without borrowing and raises savings from four months towards six.
S2.feel: Anxious, which is unusual for her, as she's normally the calm one.
S2.quote: I've always been the early one, but in two years being early is just being slightly less late.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture takes away Priya's usual advantage of being early, and she knows it. Her fear is less about robots than about big contractors with capital. She still acts quickly, but defensively, and refuses to borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something real if you start now. Small farms will need someone they trust to set the machines up. I'd say it at the discussion group and on the forums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to become that person. Not a big contractor, just the one people ring. It's risky, but I'm 27 with no kids, so if I'm going to take a risk, it's now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go part time at Westholm by next year and build the robot setup business properly, starting with the ten farms I'd scout for. I'd put about five thousand of savings into kit and a van. And I'd do a short course in farm robotics to have something on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going part time is a big risk. How is it different from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like the risk I'd take anyway. Two years forces you. Five years lets you choose, and choosing is the bit I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine, she trusts me with money. My landlord might be less fine if the first year's slow. I'd be eating a lot of pasta in 2028, and I'd be fine with that.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build something real if you start now, because small farms will need someone they trust to set the machines up. I'd say that at the discussion group and on the forums.
S3.think: I think five years is long enough for me to become the person farms ring for robot setup. It's risky, but at 27 with no children, now is the time for risk.
S3.do: Goes part time at the farm next year and builds a robot setup business starting with farms she already scouts for. Puts about five thousand of savings into kit and a van and takes a short farm robotics course.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good, motivating way.
S3.quote: I'd be eating a lot of pasta in 2028, and I'd be fine with that.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Priya would take a deliberate risk, and she links that choice to her life stage. Choosing, she says, is what she's good at; being forced is not. She expects a lean first year and seems almost to look forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best warning any industry's ever had, so use it. I'd say it a lot, probably too much. Young farmers should be learning this now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty. I'd build the business slowly, maybe hire a couple of people, maybe a small fleet. By 2036 I'd be 37 and hopefully running something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay full time at Westholm for two more years while the side business grows. Then I'd go out on my own. I'd invest in kit year by year instead of all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually quite excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI can do almost any work by 2036, can it run your business too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest worry. If the robots can do almost anything, then eventually they can set themselves up too, and I'm just the last person who knew how. But that's ten years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else do you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, and the hoeing gangs we hire every summer. I'd want to hire some of them if the business grew. Ten years is time to teach someone like Marcus, if he wanted it.

S4.say: I'd say this is the best warning any industry has ever had, so people should use it. Young farmers should be learning the machines now.
S4.think: I think ten years is plenty to grow my own business slowly, maybe with a couple of staff and a small fleet. By 2036 I'd hope to be running something of my own.
S4.do: Stays full time at the farm for two more years while growing the side business, then goes out on her own. Invests in kit year by year rather than all at once.
S4.quote: If the robots can do almost anything, then eventually they can set themselves up too, and I'm just the last person who knew how.
S4.fieldNote: The decade suits Priya's appetite for building something. She sees clearly that AGI could eventually do her business's work too, but keeps it at arm's length. She'd like to bring Marcus and the summer hoeing workers with her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being early stops mattering and the big contractors win on money. What would help is cheap start-up loans for small rural businesses, and rules so that the robot companies have to let independent people service their machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm scared of being wrong. I am a bit. I'd rather sell the shovels than dig, and in farming the shovels are about to get very clever.

headlineQuote: I'd rather sell the shovels than dig, and in farming the shovels are about to get very clever.
portrait: Priya Weber, 27, is operations lead at Westholm, a family company farm with potatoes, sugar beet, wheat and a 300-sow pig unit, and she already runs a weeding robot trial. She uses AI every day and talks in figures, and she'd be slightly restless if AI fizzled. Steady change excites her and she'd start a drone scouting side business. The two-year picture makes her anxious because being early stops mattering against big contractors, but with five or ten years she'd build her own robot setup business while she's young and free to take the risk.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to build her business and big contractors with money would win.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap start-up loans for small rural businesses and rules letting independent people service the robot makers' machines.
